summary: This Hurricane Wiki page, adapted from English Wikipedia under the GNU Free Documentation License, describes South Atlantic tropical cyclones as rare storms in the south half of the Atlantic Ocean. It attributes their rarity to high wind shear and limited space for formation, gives a November to April season peaking in March, and explains the Q and SL identifiers used for these storms. The note's content is mainly a table of contents listing eleven named or classified storms from 1974 to Akará, plus a Names section; the individual storm accounts are not included in the clipped text.
one_line: Overview of rare South Atlantic tropical cyclones, their season, identifiers, and a list of notable storms, adapted from Wikipedia.
key_facts: A South Atlantic tropical cyclone is a rare cyclone that occurs in the south half of the Atlantic Ocean.
South Atlantic tropical cyclones are rare due to high wind shear and lack of space for the cyclones to form.
If there was a Hurricane Season or Cyclone Season for the South Atlantic, it would last from November to April, with March being its peak.
South Atlantic cyclones would be given identifiers Q or SL, for example INVEST 90Q or Tropical Depression 1-SL.
The page's first section, Tropical or Subtropical cyclones, lists eleven storms, starting with the Subtropical Cyclone of March 1974.
The listed storms include the Angola Tropical Storm of 1991, Tropical Cyclone of January 2004, and Cyclone Catarina.
Other listed storms include the Tropical Storm of February 2006, Subtropical Storm of January 2009, and Tropical Storm Anita.
The later listed storms are the Subtropical Storm of November 2010, Subtropical Storm Arani, Tropical Storm Iba, and Tropical Storm Akará.
The page's second section is titled Names.
The page states it uses content from Wikipedia, with the original article at en:wikipedia:South Atlantic tropical cyclone.
The text of Wikipedia is available under the GNU Free Documentation License, as with Hurricane Wiki.
The page is hosted on the Hurricane Wiki on Fandom, in the category South Atlantic Tropical Cyclones.
